notes.meaning: The Lord calls out in a loud, commanding voice to the heavenly beings appointed to punish Jerusalem. These executioners are angels prepared to carry out God's judgment, each holding a destructive weapon. Because the people ignored God's quiet warnings, they must now face His anger.

Six executioners arrive from the north gate, the direction where the Babylonians would attack and where idols had been set up. Walking with them is a seventh figure dressed in priestly linen, carrying a writer's kit to protect God's people before the punishment begins. They all stand by the bronze altar, showing that this judgment is offered as a holy sacrifice to God's justice.

differ.view: Many commentators identify the man in linen as the preincarnate Christ serving as an intercessory High Priest, while others see him as a high-ranking angel.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the seven figures reflect ancient Near Eastern motifs, such as the Babylonian grouping of seven planetary deities or the heavenly scribe god.

notes.meaning: The bright cloud of God's glory rises from its place above the winged cherubim and moves to the doorway of the temple. This movement signals that the Lord is preparing to leave His house because the people have driven Him away through their sins. From the threshold, God calls to the man in linen to give him his assignment.

God tells the man in linen to walk throughout Jerusalem and place a mark on the foreheads of everyone who groans and weeps over the wicked things done there. These faithful people do not join in the evil, but mourn over how God's name is dishonored. The mark protects them from destruction, just like the lamb's blood protected Israelite homes during the first Passover.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church fathers and Catholic interpreters saw this mark, the Hebrew letter taw which originally looked like a cross, as a foreshadowing of the cross of Christ and Christian signing with the cross.

notes.meaning: The Lord directs the other six men to follow right behind the scribe and strike the city without showing any mercy. God cares for His faithful people first, but once they are safe, judgment falls on everyone else. The executioners are strictly told not to spare anyone who has refused to turn back to God.

The executioners receive orders to slaughter anyone without the mark, regardless of age or gender, but they are forbidden to touch anyone who bears it. This judgment begins at God's own sanctuary, starting with the elders who practiced idolatry right outside the temple. Those who enjoyed the greatest spiritual privileges and led others into sin face God's justice first.

God commands the executioners to defile the temple courts by filling them with the bodies of the slain. The people had already made the sanctuary unclean by worshipping idols there, so God treats it as an unholy place. The executioners obey and go out from the temple into the rest of the city to carry out the sentence.

Seeing the terrible slaughter all around him, Ezekiel feels as though he is the only person left alive in the temple. He falls facedown on the ground to pray and plead for mercy. He cries out to God, asking if the Lord's anger against Jerusalem will completely wipe out what remains of Israel.

The Lord answers Ezekiel by showing that the punishment is completely fair because the nation's sins are overwhelmingly great. The land is filled with murder, and the law courts are twisted and corrupt. The people falsely tell themselves that God has abandoned them and cannot see the evil they do.

Because the people showed no mercy and claimed that God was blind to their crimes, the Lord refuses to look on them with pity. He will bring the full penalty of their own choices down upon their heads. True justice requires that those who stubbornly continue in sin receive the fruit of their ways.

The man dressed in linen returns to report that he has completely carried out God's command. Every believer who grieved over sin was successfully marked and protected from the slaughter. This shows that God's promises never fail, and His servants are faithful in preserving those who belong to Him.
